headline: Mimicry is looking like something you're not—deception as survival strategy
universal_truth: Appearance shapes perception; looking like something can be as powerful as being something
fun_facts: The viceroy butterfly mimics the toxic monarch so predators avoid eating it
Some harmless snakes have evolved to look like venomous coral snakes
Orchids mimic female wasps so well that male wasps try to mate with them, spreading pollen
discussion_questions: When do you present yourself differently than you feel?
When is mimicry strategic versus deceptive?
What signals do you send that shape how others perceive you?

hook.title: Welcome
hook.script: The harmless viceroy looks exactly like the toxic monarch butterfly. Predators can't tell the difference—so they avoid both. Mimicry is nature's fraud: looking like something you're not to gain advantage. Appearance is power.

options.text: I want to learn something new
options.response: Perfect. Curiosity is the first step to understanding. Let's explore this together.
That curiosity is exactly what we need. Let's dive in and discover something amazing.

cliff.title: The Question
cliff.script: Mimicry seems like cheating—pretending to be something you're not. But it's incredibly effective. What does mimicry teach us about perception?

options.text: Mimicry works because observers respond to signals, not reality—if you send the right signals, you get treated like what you resemble, regardless of what you actually are
options.response: Yes. Perception is based on signals. If you look toxic, you're treated as toxic. If you look harmless, you're treated as harmless. Signals often matter more than substance.
It fools careful predators too—the risk of being wrong outweighs the benefit of testing...

q1.title: Signal Exploitation
q1.script: Predators learn 'orange and black = toxic.' Mimics exploit this learning. They don't need to be toxic—just send the same signal. Learning can be hacked through signal matching.
q1.prompt: What's your first impression of "Signal Exploitation"?

options.text: This confirms what I already knew
options.response: Great foundation! Now let's build on that knowledge with something you might not expect...
Perfect starting point! This insight will connect to even more surprising facts ahead.

q2.title: Costs and Limits
q2.script: Mimicry has limits. If too many mimics exist compared to genuine examples, predators learn the signal is unreliable. The strategy works only while mimics remain relatively rare.
q2.prompt: How does this connect to what you already know?

options.response: Exactly. These connections are how knowledge becomes understanding.

options.text: I need to think about this more
options.response: That's a good instinct. Deep understanding takes time. The next fact will help clarify.

q3.title: Human Mimicry
q3.script: Humans mimic too: dress codes, accent shifting, credential signaling. We send signals that shape how we're perceived. Understanding this is power—both to use signals and to see through them.
q3.prompt: What surprises you most about this?

options.text: I never thought about it this way
options.response: That shift in perspective is exactly the point. New angles reveal new truths.
That's learning in action. When understanding shifts, you're really getting it.

wisdom.title: Today's Wisdom
wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: Appearance shapes perception. Looking like something can be as powerful as being something. Understand the signals you send.
wisdom.prompt: What resonates most with you today?

options.response: That central truth will stay with you. Let it guide your thinking.
Application is where knowledge becomes wisdom. That's the real learning.

outro.title: See You Tomorrow
outro.script: That's Day 251. Tomorrow, we'll explore species that help each other—symbiosis. Until then, notice what signals you're sending.
outro.prompt: Before you go—what will you take from today?

options.response: Reflection deepens learning. Let these ideas simmer in your mind.
Teaching others is the best way to learn. You've already begun the ripple.

growTrack.title: Signal Audit - What Are You Communicating?
growTrack.learning_objective: Understand signals sent through appearance and behavior
growTrack.activity: What signals do you send through appearance, credentials, behavior? Are they accurate or mimicry? Both have uses—but know which you're doing. Also: what signals do you read from others that might be mimicry?
